A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same subobject-tokenization research, despite substantial revision. Their text and visuals support reliable comparison. v2 has no appendix; v3 includes readable Appendices A–D.

before.justification: v2 reports original CLEVR captioning experiments, including training curves and object-attribute/count accuracies on 2,000 test images (Section 3, Figure 4).

after.justification: v3 reports original segmentation, computational-efficiency and downstream VLM experiments, with additional ablations and analyses in the appendices (Sections 4–5, Appendices B–C).

M1.justification: The boundary-prediction idea persists, but v3 presents a 3.7M-parameter SegFormer-b0/watershed EPOC pipeline, compared with v2's 84.6M-parameter DirectSAM. More substantially, SeqAE's learned autoencoding is replaced by pooled image features, bounding-box-plus-mask position encoding and MLP fusion (v2 Sections 2–3; v3 Sections 3.2.3 and 5.1).

E1.justification: v3 adds ImageNet-1K recognition, ShareGPT4V/Pixmo-cap detailed captioning, and intrinsic object/part segmentation evaluation on COCO/COCONut, ADE20K, PPP and PartImageNet++. SA-1B and CLEVR-derived captioning are retained; CLEVR captions additionally describe color. This substantially broadens the represented domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 compares its MobileSAM-v2/SeqAE VLM with one patch-based baseline. v3's downstream comparisons include patch, Mask2Former-tiny/large and SLIC against EPOC. Its intrinsic comparisons additionally evaluate OneFormer, SAM ViT-B/H, FastSAM and MobileSAMv2 (Figures 4–5, Table 1).

E3.justification: CLEVR evaluation changes from 2,000 to 5,000 held-out images, 10 to 30 training epochs, and batch size 32 to 512. Phi-2 with LoRA is replaced by fully fine-tuned SmolLM2/Llama configurations. v3 also introduces token-budget sweeps, intrinsic segmentation metrics and throughput protocols, while replacing caption-attribute accuracy reporting with validation perplexity (Appendices A–C).

E4.justification: v3 adds embedding ablations and token-truncation experiments, using random removal for patches and smallest-segment removal for adaptive tokenizers (Figure 6). It also analyzes segmentation granularity, token-size distributions and inference scaling with process count (Figures 7–13). v2 contains no comparable analysis suite.

E5.justification: v3 Section 5.3 newly clarifies that each plotted VLM point represents an individual run. This is a limited disclosure about result aggregation, not evidence of increased replication. Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2's CLEVR accuracy entries, including 11% patch versus 63% subobject count accuracy, are removed. v3 reports new segmentation, perplexity/token-budget, ablation and efficiency results; Table 1 gives maximum throughput of 17.1 FPS for EPOC versus 12.2 for FastSAM. These are new or replaced results under revised settings, not same-setting improvements over v2.

T1.justification: v3 introduces a formal token-index-map formulation and defines token monosemanticity, including its erosion-based operational test (Section 2.1, Section 4.2, Appendix B). These are limited formal additions. The O(N)-versus-O(1) boundary-prediction argument already appears in v2; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The contribution shifts from DirectSAM/SeqAE and preliminary CLEVR learning advantages to EPOC and systematic comparison of adaptive tokenizers. v3 adds central claims about morphology alignment, monosemanticity, token efficiency and advantages over object-level tokenization across recognition and captioning settings (abstract, introduction and conclusion).

C2.justification: v3 develops explanations linking polysemantic tokens to infrequent semantic mixtures and truncation robustness to long-tailed token sizes. Appendix D newly identifies limitations involving thin structures, evaluated LLM scale, segmentation latency and loss of within-token spatial detail. These substantially extend v2's interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C replace the DirectSAM/SeqAE/Phi-2 recipes with EPOC/VLM implementation information and add comparator checkpoint identifiers, segmentation settings, metric tolerances, optimizer/warmup details, precision and token caps. Conversely, v2's own code/model and demonstration links are omitted; this does not establish that those resources were withdrawn.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning beyond the subword analogy and SAM. It adds cognitive recognition-by-components research, tokenization/compression studies, and direct discussion of prior superpixel tokenizers, slot attention and token pooling. Section 6 distinguishes separate segmentation from feature-based grouping and explains compatibility with token-embedding research.

P1.justification: The main narrative is extensively rewritten and reorganized into preliminaries, adaptive segmentation, separate intrinsic/extrinsic evaluations and related work. Implementation material is redistributed into expanded appendices, and terminology and contribution framing are substantially revised. This exceeds routine editing or renumbering.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the introductory analogy and SeqAE/LVLM graphics with a watershed schematic, comparative segmentation panels, an efficiency table and extensive evaluation/ablation plots. The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with further displays in the appendices. These are substantial visual and layout changes.

improvement.justification: v2's downstream evidence uses MobileSAM-v2 on synthetic CLEVR, explicitly deferring DirectSAM evaluation. v3 directly tests EPOC's segmentation quality, computational cost and downstream usefulness against relevant alternatives, with token-budget comparisons, ablations and substantive limitations (Sections 4–5, Appendices B–D). Replacing attribute/count accuracies with perplexity reduces direct semantic interpretability, and project links are lost, but resolving the proposed tokenizer's validation gap substantially strengthens the paper.
